en: The Bodhicaryāvatāra, Fascicle One.
Compiled in verse by the Noble Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna at Jālandhara in Central India, the Land of the West.
Just as the essence of the Buddha’s wondrous Dharma is boundless, the sons of the Buddha, with upright minds, take refuge and pay homage;
may the Buddha’s nectar-like precepts cover and protect them, and I now praise and explain them all in accordance with the Dharma.
This teaching is neither unprecedented nor is it my own exclusive possession;
when there was no distinction between self and other, I then contemplated and observed for myself.
When observing with such a resolve, it enables this goodness of mine to increase;
at that time, seeing this Sahā world, I realize that this is indeed that Buddha, the World-Honored One.
This realm is difficult to encounter even for a single moment; having been born as a human, you should rejoice.
Yet, if one contemplates and departs from the bodhicitta, how could one possibly attain this state again?
Just as when the night is shrouded in darkness by clouds, a flash of lightning reveals its brilliance for a moment;
so too is the majestic power of the Buddha: one who gives rise to the thought [of awakening] for even a moment attains merit.
Therefore, even if one's goodness is slight and one's strength inferior, it can destroy the power of great evil karma;
likewise, if one arouses the bodhicitta, this courageous diligence can transcend that [evil].
Contemplating throughout immeasurable and boundless eons, I have seen all Buddhas proclaim this truth:
that by finding joy where there was no joy, one increases and delivers infinite multitudes of beings.
For the sake of all sentient beings dwelling amidst manifold sufferings, may they be freed from hundreds of thousands of fears and afflictions,
and may they experience hundreds of thousands of kinds of great joy, remaining forever inseparable from the bodhicitta.
Though that Son of the Sugata remains amidst the fetters and veils, wandering in saṃsāra without attachment,
if he utters the thought of awakening for even a single moment, gods and humans rejoice and all take refuge in him.
If one upholds even an impure image, it is likened to a Buddha-relic image that is priceless;
like a medicinal transformation that is pervasive and firm, it is equal to the cultivation and maintenance of the wondrous bodhicitta.
The jewel of the bodhicitta possesses boundless efficacy; its value is such that nothing in the world can serve as a metaphor for it.
May it cause all those who are companions on the path—the practitioners and their guides—to uphold it with firm resolve.
The plantain tree produces fruit though it lacks substance; once it has produced fruit, the plantain perishes.
Yet the Bodhicitta-tree is pure; it constantly bears supreme fruits without ever being exhausted.
Having already committed various violent and evil karmic deeds, one is liberated in an instant by relying on the bodhicitta;
since there is no great fear when relying with such courage, why do those deluded sentient beings not rely upon it?
Just as the great fire at the end of an eon, in a single instant, incinerates the fuel of sinful karma,
so too is one who praises the Compassionate Honored One with immeasurable words called a wise person of excellence.
That mind of various conceptualizations is equalized through right knowledge;
with the mind of the vow for enlightenment, one practices the conduct of enlightenment.
It is like a traveler wishing to go, whose various distinctions are thus explained.
Having explained through the discernment of wisdom, one acts in accordance with the application of that wisdom.
The aspirational mind for enlightenment and its great fruit are like saṃsāra;
because of merit, they are uninterrupted, just like the intent of those practices.
If those infinite realms of sentient beings were liberated,
and their minds were equal to his own, his vow for enlightenment would not regress;
yet they sleep soundly and remain deeply mired in delusion.
The flow of merit is interrupted, Metaphorically like a void where nothing exists.
Subāhu asks this: for sentient beings of inferior mind who have attained birth in liberation, Is it for themselves, or for the Tathāgata?
He then reflects upon how to heal and remove the suffering of sentient beings;
once their suffering has been exhausted, they shall attain boundless merit.
Since the suffering of sentient beings is boundless, how can it be healed?
May each and every one find peace and happiness, and attain boundless merit.
How can one benefit one's parents, as well as one's kinsmen and retinue?
May they obtain gods and seers, and pure-practicing brahmins.
Thus, those sentient beings have emerged from the sleep of the past;
they do not desire their own benefit, but wish only for the benefit of others.
How could such supreme jewels among sentient beings, so rare to encounter, ever come to be born?
Various ways of benefiting others, not merely self-interest;
the seeds of joy for the world, the medicine for the world;
the jewel of the mind and its merit—how can one describe them?
How can all sentient beings obtain every happiness?
By generating the bodhicitta and making offerings to the Tathāgata.
To be deluded by attachment to pleasure is likened to harboring enmity and resentment.
Detachment and its accompaniments all arise from one's own mind.
If one seeks happiness, there are boundless seeds of suffering;
by accumulating various virtues and joys, all sufferings are eliminated.
To destroy the causes of delusion—how is this excellently attained?
By relying upon those spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), such merit is thereby obtained.
If one dedicates the benefit [one has performed], they will surely respond with praise.
One who performs good deeds without seeking profit is called a bodhisattva.
If one practices generosity by giving even a small amount of food, cultivating virtue as an offering to the world,
then even a gift as small as a mosquito or a gnat will yield the joy of half a day.
How does one attain the state of the Muni?
It is by vowing to deliver all sentient beings to the end; though sentient beings are as inexhaustible as space, one seeks the perfection of omniscience.
O Son of the Buddha, contemplate in stillness: if afflictions arise, they are created by one's own mind;
yet when such afflictions repeatedly arise, doubt is born once more, and the Buddha says that such a person falls into hell.
If a follower of the Buddha gives rise to the bodhicitta, The power of great sins is extinguished and supreme fruits are attained.
I now take refuge in the mani-heart, Which delivers sentient beings and brings them happiness.
With a mind of reverence, he offered those mani-jewels as an offering to the Tathāgata and to the pure, wondrous Jewel of the Dharma; the ocean of the Buddha’s merit is boundless.
All the exquisite flowers found in the world, Even the finest fruits and medicinal decoctions,
And all precious gems and clear waters— I offer them all as worship to bring you joy.
The treasures of the mountains and all manner of jewels, the delightful groves and places of tranquility,
trees adorned with flowering vines and radiant light, and branches bending low with clusters of fruit— these flourish in abundance.
In the human realm and the heavens, there are fragrant unguents and incenses, even the kalpa-trees and jewel-trees;
the pond waters are pure and further adorned, while the geese and swans utter beautiful sounds that are most pleasing to the mind.
Grains grow spontaneously without being sown; each is adorned separately as offerings, vast in measure equal to the realm of empty space—all these are fully enjoyed.
These offerings I now present, together with my children and others, I offer to the supreme Buddha, the Muni;
for the sake of not abandoning me, may you accept this most excellent offering out of your great compassion.
Lacking merit and being utterly destitute, I have no other offering whatsoever;
now, reflecting for the sake of both myself and others, I pray that the Buddha will accept this gift according to my humble capacity.

I offer my very self to all Buddhas; May my own body and others pervade everywhere, Blessing me as a superior being among sentient beings, And may I constantly transform and guide sentient beings through the Buddha's teaching.
Having received the empowerment of the Tathāgata, I shall transform and benefit sentient beings without fear;
all past karmic offenses are now completely abandoned, and future transgressions shall no longer be committed.
The place of jewel radiance is most delightful; adorned with celestial canopies, it honors the Tathāgata.
Pure and luminous as crystal, various wondrous halls are prepared for fragrant ablutions.
A great precious vase filled with fragrant water, further adorned with various exquisite flowers that please the mind, shall bathe the stainless body of the Tathāgata;
I shall then offer hymns of praise and present songs and music.
With pure incense and most excellent garments, used as a canopy to cover that one of supreme form, I now offer these superior robes;
may the Buddha, out of compassion, graciously accept them.
Various kinds of soft and exquisite celestial robes, the most supreme among all adornments,
are offered to the Tathāgata and Samantabhadra, as well as to Mañjuśrī and Avalokiteśvara.
Observing the precepts is for the sake of protecting the mind; protect it so that it becomes firm and strong.
If this mind cannot be protected, how can one protect the precepts?
It is like an intoxicated elephant that has not been subdued; it feels no concern for its own pain.
Relaxing like a rutting elephant, one shall invite rebirth in the Avīci hell and other realms.
Always hold fast to the rope of mindfulness to bind the elephant of the mind;
thus one may escape the fear of negligence and attain all peace and happiness.
If one can bind the single mind, one can bind all things;
if one subdues the single mind, all things are naturally subdued.
Whether it be lions, bears, tigers, or wolves, or yakṣas and rākṣasas—
All the hell-wardens are none other than one's own enemies.
If one fears all such enemies, know that this accumulation of boundless suffering arises solely from the mind;
thus the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has truly taught.
The various instruments of suffering in hell, as well as the glowing iron balls and the like—
who created them, and from what were they born?
They are all produced by greed, hatred, and delusion.
Because of those sinful minds, the Buddha appears in all worlds;
because the mind within the three realms is extinguished, there is therefore no fear.
If one practiced generosity in the past, one will not be poor in this present life.
Do not be distressed by present poverty; why regret the past?
If a person’s mind, even for a small portion, practices the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), the resulting fruit is said to be equal to all other acts of generosity.
If a person’s mind observes the precepts, why begrudge and kill any being?
The enemy that is the mind of anger—if one were to slaughter them all, they would equal the expanse of space.
The great earth is boundless in measure; with what hide could it ever be covered?
A sandal made from a small portion of leather covers the feet wherever one goes;
likewise, the nature of the "external self" is the same—what can anyone do about it?
One should merely exhort one's own mind, and the external self will submit of its own accord.
Though one’s body be poor and devoid of merit, the fruit corresponds to one’s own conduct;
if with a generous mind one gives even a single garment, one will experience the resulting fruit and increase in merit.
If one practices all deeds in this way, never abandoning them from the mind, [the fruit shall likewise follow].
All thoughts devoid of benefit, And all that is false and deceptive, should be shunned.
All mental qualities and spiritual wealth Should be observed with secrecy;
By leaving suffering behind and attaining peace, One shall transcend the world.
How should I practice? Practice consists solely in guarding the mind; therefore, I observe the mind and constantly provide it with protection.
Just as one would protect a wound on a monkey’s body, I guard the mind with single-minded focus.
Such are the evils among humans; one must always guard the mind.
Fearing the sores of suffering and affliction, I constantly protect it with a single-minded focus;
by destroying the *Saṃghāta* hell, the sores of the mind will then be free from fear.
Always practicing such conduct, one does not commit the evils of humanity;
by not committing human transgressions, one is naturally free from fear.
Desiring to exhaust my very life for the sake of others, I shall offer service through beneficial actions.
Though my body and life may perish one by one, may my virtuous mind never retreat.
Desiring to guard my mind, I now join my palms in single-minded devotion;
within every thought-moment, I shall protect it through every possible means.
Just as one who is gravely ill cannot endure any activity,
so too is a distracted mind incapable of any task.
With a mind that is scattered and unstable, even hearing, reflection, and investigation [fail].
Just as a leaking vessel cannot hold water,
so too a person of much learning who possesses faults such as lack of faith, lack of skillful means,
and an unstable mind, incurs the fault of failing to attain tranquility.
Because the mind is not resolute, it is seized by the thieves of delusion;
whatever merit and goodness one possesses, they steal and cause one to fall into evil realms.
Because the many bandits of affliction and the attachments of Māra gain the opportunity, [the mind is lost].
Arising from Māra, it destroys one's virtuous life.
Guarding the gateway of the mental faculty, evil cannot drag one away;
by recollecting the suffering of those transgressions, one subsequently attains stable abiding.
Excellent is following the teacher’s instruction; thereby wholesome thoughts arise.
One should serve the teacher who provides such counsel, providing for them with a single-minded heart.
Toward all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one’s mind should be resolute in every moment.
When fear arises, bring mindfulness to mind; let compassion appear before you.
If the dust of worldly thoughts unsettles the mind, it will depart and depart, never to return again.
Yet if one can guard the gateways of the senses and protect them so they do not scatter, [the mind remains stable].
I shall now protect this mind, dwelling constantly in this manner;
like a tree without roots, no evil branches or leaves shall grow.
When the eyes perceive forms and appearances, one knows them to be empty, false, and unreal.
Constantly contemplate each and every thing; therefore, do not become attached.
Observe through the faculty of vision, and by observing, bring about freedom from delusion.
Once you have observed that which has come before you, remain at ease and welcome it with goodness.
When one wishes to travel but does not know the way, fear arises as they look toward the four quarters;
once they have definitively known the direction, they proceed.
The practice of the wise is likewise: they contemplate both what has preceded and what follows.
Whether it be good or evil, such matters do not perish.
Since one does not abide in this body, what else could one do apart from it?
How then can one abide in this body?
One should further observe the middle;
observing the inner mind is likewise so. Employing various skillful means, one takes the Dharma as a great pillar to bind it so that it does not escape.
With such an intention, one should contemplate where I abide;
all consciousnesses are likewise thus—restrain them so that they remain for a single moment.
If you fear the power of karma and seek to attain happiness, [you must practice accordingly].
Cultivating those perfections of generosity and ethical discipline, up to great relinquishment and so forth—
if one cultivates the causes of awakening, one should not dwell on their distinctions;
rather, cultivating one's own mind exclusively, one should give rise to this view:
Thus cultivating all virtues, one gives rise to no fear,
and causes all afflictions to certainly not increase.
Various correct teachings are seen to be exceedingly numerous.
Observing and contemplating all things with full comprehension, one shatters the net of doubt and attains the fruit.
Like grass that has been cut down, one who recollects the Buddha and is able to endure through the precepts—
practicing this way for even a single moment— will obtain a most excellent fruit.
If you wish to attain complete mastery over all correct teachings,
you should contemplate and observe your own mind and constantly cultivate diligence.
Like wood that is insentient, it is without speech and without action.
Seeing one's own mind is likewise; one must certainly bring it to such a state.
If the mind gives rise to contempt, like a person intoxicated with delusion, seeking only self-praise and reputation, that is not the practitioner.
If others should direct slander toward me, claiming I am possessed of anger,
delusion, and the like, may my mind remain ever as steady as wood. Like wood,
it shall not discriminate between gain and loss, honor and dishonor, or praise and blame.
Nor for the sake of kinsmen, nor even for service and the like;
seeking no self-interest but desiring only the benefit of all,
I therefore declare that my mind shall remain steadfast and constant as a block of wood.
Abiding with single-minded focus like a block of wood, toward teachers, parents, friends,
and even regarding the three types of action, one gives rise to neither hatred, attachment, nor fear.
Observing the afflictions as being like space, one remains unattached.
One should be courageous and steadfast, maintaining this practice as a constant habit.
Without shame or fear, one should single-mindedly seek others’ respect;
dwelling purely in samādhi, one shall be honored by all.
Though dwelling in the state of childhood, I do not cause others to feel anger or vexation, nor do I myself become angry with them; my compassion remains ever thus.
I uphold dhyāna, causing the mind to be constantly tranquil.
For the sake of all sentient beings, may you always abide in a state free from fault.
In every thought-moment and for even a brief instant, let the duration of practice be supreme;
thus maintaining this resolve, remain as immovable as Mount Sumeru.
As the vulture craves flesh without satiety, so too does the person crave merit;
if one does not practice with body and mind, how can one attain liberation?
How can one guard the body and the mind?
At all times you must exert yourself; what are you doing now? Each of you should focus your mind with single-minded devotion.
Deluded and foolish, you fail to restrain yourselves, vainly craving this wooden body.
Since this body is composed of impurities, why do you instead feel such attachment to it?
A chain of bones held together by flesh, adorned with outer skin;
realizing this for oneself, one becomes free from craving. Through the blade of wisdom, one is liberated.
By dissecting the various parts of the body, one causes the inner essence to be seen.
Examine and contemplate with scrutiny: how can one perceive a person?
Contemplate thus with a single mind; when scrutinized with truth, no person is seen.
Why then do you greedily cherish and protect this impure body?
Dwelling in the womb, one consumes impurities; upon leaving the womb, one drinks blood and milk.
Since such food and drink are not [fit for a noble being], how could one create this body?
Jackals, vultures, and the like greedily consume it, making no distinction between good and evil.
If you desire to love your body as others do, yet its enjoyment only results in the burden of karma—
if you merely protect this body in such a way that you lack compassion and patience until death,
no different from a jackal or a vulture— why do you constantly act in this manner?
When the body dies, consciousness does not remain; how could clothing and food possibly stay?
When the body departs, consciousness must surely go; why then be greedy for enjoyments?
Therefore, now apply your mind so as not to crave such things.
Thus, by not remaining far removed from them, one incurs all those unwholesome states.
It is like a person born with a body who seeks to perfect its limbs;
yet though they receive this body, their wisdom does not increase, and they wander in saṃsāra, needlessly exhausting themselves.
Toward those who are friends or foes in the world, one should first comfort them with a pleasant countenance;
thus constantly exercising self-restraint, one should never let such thoughts of the mind be abandoned.
One should not laugh with a loud voice, nor should one toss one's sitting mat about in play.
Knock gently at another's door; maintain constant faith and self-restraint.
Like a thief, a cat, or a heron seeking its prey, one should move silently;
so too should one cultivate the mind, remaining free from coarseness and violence.
One avoids what others detest and speaks nothing that is unrighteous or profitless;
thus one always gains the disciples who hold one’s words as supreme and revere them with love.
Whatever one says, upon hearing it, they all exclaim, "Excellent!"
When observing another performing meritorious deeds, praise them so as to bring them joy.
Speak of their virtues in private; when they hear it, their heart will surely rejoice.
When you wish to praise someone, first observe their virtuous conduct.
Cultivate all joyful and auspicious deeds; it is difficult to find such sincere hearts.
Diligently cultivate the virtue of benefiting others, and you shall receive the retribution of happiness.
Abandon hatred and attachment for the sake of suffering, as they lead to great misery in future lives.
"I shall not abide in this suffering; in future lives there will be great happiness.
With gentle words and a soft voice, one who speaks from the root of compassion brings joy upon being heard;
by revealing matters that are pleasing to others, one should believe in truthful speech.
Constantly feeling compassion for sentient beings, protecting them as one protects one's own eyes,
and abiding in reality for their sake, one will surely attain Buddhahood.
Once that reality is attained, each shall benefit their friends.
Cultivating merit for even a single moment brings great peace and happiness free from suffering.
By cultivating merit with earnest diligence, one attains it through constant practice;
neither flaunting nor concealing it—who would say that such deeds are equal to others?
The perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) and the others are sublime and supreme;
separate practices are not supreme, for they lack the benefit of others and the absence of detachment.
The Buddha thus benefits others, being ever-constant and earnest in his concern.
Within the teaching of the Tathāgata, one perceives those acts of compassion.
When the Teacher of the Three Realms entered parinirvāṇa, he distinguished the matters concerning renunciants:
that food is either permissible or impermissible, and that they must not be separated from their three robes and so forth.
Seeking to attain the wondrous Dharma-body, one does not cause suffering to sentient beings;
toward sentient beings in this manner, one attains fulfillment according to one's will.
One should practice relinquishment even at the cost of one’s life; that relinquishment must be impartial.
Compassion should be pure, and its fruition will naturally be perfected.
With a pure mind, one honors the Dharma; one does not carry weapons or staves, nor hold umbrellas over one's head, and remains free from all acts of disrespect.
For the sake of men and women, he preaches the Dharma that is profound and vast;
without distinguishing between superior and inferior persons, he causes them to value equality.
As for the Dharma that is not vast, as well as unrighteous conduct—
One should stay far away from those who show no respect and take delight in preaching the Mahāyāna.
One must not discard tooth-sticks, nasal mucus, or saliva on clean ground;
likewise, one must not discharge excrement or urine into pure water or in a clean dwelling.
Do not eat with a mouthful full; do not make noise while eating;
do not speak while eating, nor open your mouth too wide.
When sitting, do not let your feet dangle; when walking, do not swing your arms.
Do not ride in the same vehicle with women, nor sit or lie down together with them.
Regarding all such improper acts, people will see them and feel displeasure;
once everyone has observed them, they will distance themselves and show no respect.
When asked for directions by others on the road, one must not point with a single finger;
rather, one should point with both hands to indicate where the path leads.
In all one's movements and steps, one should not dangle the arms or make noise.
Nor should you snap your fingers recklessly; maintain such deportment.
Although the Master has already passed into extinction, you should train in the four modes of conduct.
By reverently upholding the precepts and practicing without negligence, you will certainly attain the fruits of sainthood.
The practices of the Bodhisattvas are immeasurable, and what they teach is boundless;
one should, with a pure mind, resolutely practice them.
Dividing each day and night into three periods, one should apply oneself accordingly.
Practicing the path, one universally repents; Abiding in the Buddha’s bodhicitta.
May bodhicitta abide within oneself, And likewise cause others to attain it.
The Son of the Buddha abides in the training precepts, Holding them thus with a single mind.
The essence of the Buddha’s precepts is pure; Not even a hair’s breadth of fault is seen.
If one constantly practices in this manner, That merit shall be immeasurable.
Since beginningless time for the sake of sentient beings, One has practiced deeds without distinction.
Thus, for the sake of sentient beings, one should transform them so that all may awaken.
Know that a spiritual friend is like one's own life and must not be forsaken;
the Bodhisattva precepts are supreme, and the Mahāyāna Dharma is likewise.
Liberation depends on training under a teacher, through which one can give rise to auspiciousness.
The Buddhas have taught the Sūtra of Wisdom; by reading it, one perceives the Dharma of the precepts.
If a person’s mind guards the precepts, all that they practice will be clearly seen.
Whether in body or in mind, one should observe with subtle discernment.
What can be said as a metaphor for one who recites with the mouth but does not practice with the body?
They are like a gravely ill person who speaks only of the power of medicine.
In the *Gaganagañja-sūtra*, the *Maulī-bhūmi* is explained;
as for the collection of morality and concentration, it is as extensively taught in that sūtra.
The noble Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna has single-mindedly compiled [this work].
Wherever one may dwell, one should constantly offer worship.
*Bodhicaryāvatāra*, Scroll One.
*Bodhicaryāvatāra*, Scroll Two.
Compiled in verse by the Holy Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna;
practiced in the dense forests of Jālandhara in Central India,
where all wholesome deeds are performed, with generosity and ethical discipline as the forerunners.
Making offerings to the Tathāgata for hundreds of thousands of kalpas is inexhaustible;
practicing kṣānti (patience), one does not allow the fault of anger to arise.
Contemplating that all various entities are empty, one therefore maintains patience with a single mind.
One must not crave pleasure; guard the mind and keep it equanimous.
When the mind suffers from the disease of anger and resentment, one finds no rest and is never satisfied.
Whether it be this person or that, there are donors who provide offerings and sustenance.
Following that heart of affection and respect, do not give rise to anger or vexation.
In all matters of intimacy, do not harbor hatred or disdain;
by being free from anger toward them, one attains peace and happiness.
If one can endure such matters as these, even when facing an enemy,
and if one is able to eliminate anger, one will obtain peace and happiness in every life.
If enmity arises in the mind, there is likewise no joy in affection.
If one consumes the food of anger and affliction, there is no patience and no goodness remains uncorrupted.
That food devours my great enemy; it brings me no benefit whatsoever.
Knowing that such an enemy is not to be consumed, one’s patience is therefore firm and steadfast.
Whenever you see an enemy approaching or departing, rejoice and do not give way to anger;
if anger should arise toward an enemy, all wholesome benefits will ultimately perish.
Always maintain such a mind of forbearance, so that anger may never arise.
Abiding in patience without regard for time, resentment and enmity will not arise of their own accord.
If one cherishes oneself and does not commit the karma of harsh speech,
yet this karma of speech is not abandoned, one will later experience the suffering of enemies.
Fearing suffering yet not seeking liberation from it, one does not practice the causes for ending all suffering;
therefore, with a mind of firm endurance, one attains all forms of happiness.
That son of Nalanda, seeking liberation through false views—
Though my body be cut by knives or burned by fire, I can endure it because there is no benefit [in it].
Yet the foolish, lacking right view, undergo great suffering and affliction in vain;
since I possess the bodhicitta, why should I not endure suffering?
Mosquitoes, fleas, and bedbugs constantly suffer from hunger and thirst;
they cause great itching and vexation to people, yet one dwells in patience and does not see them.
Cold and heat, rain and wind, as well as illness, shackles, and beatings—[one endures these].
Afflicted by various sufferings and tribulations, he endured them without seeking pleasure.
As blood gushed from the killing of others, his mind remained firm and courageous;
yet when he saw the blood from his own body after it was cut, he fell down in terror and alarm.
The wise person’s mind is pure; they always fear the invasion of anger and affliction.
Holding fast against these defilements, their heart of patience remains ever courageous.
Like a snake gliding on its belly along the ground, this is a metaphor for anger subdued within the mind.
To kill them is called lacking courage; by killing them, one attains supreme victory.

The Tathāgata, the Greatly Compassionate One, out of pity for suffering, taught about saṃsāra so that people may recognize the root of their transgressions and abide in patience rather than committing harm.
What thoughts did my parents harbor? Fearing that their child might suffer drowning, they maintained a mind free from anger and distanced themselves from the retribution of great suffering.
It is like an ignorant person who causes sin to arise.
If one practices without wisdom, anger will likewise arise.
If you wish to abide in the inconceivable, you must maintain your own mind;
by cherishing it with love and respect, you shall prevent anger from arising.
If one craves those sensory objects, various transgressions arise;
due to the power of those karmic actions, one does not attain freedom.
If one does not crave those objects, their accumulation has no cause to stand.
Because the harmonious mind does not exist, there is therefore no arising.
Without craving, there is no birth; without attainment, one speaks of oneself:
"Because I have attained suchness, this arising is inconceivable."
Since that which is unborn does not arise, how could attainment exist?
By observing both self and other, one attains the remainderless extinction (*nirvāṇa*).
This mind is eternally pure, like a mani jewel that reflects whatever color it encounters.
All that is transformed arises from causes; how could there be characteristics without causes?
When past actions were being performed, what did those actions do?
Following the causes of those performed actions, one experiences results through corresponding causes.
Although all things arise from causes, those causes—good and evil—originate in the mind.
To speak of seeking the tranquility of intrinsic nature, what fault is there in this?
If one grasps at the causes of conditioned combinations, this pleasure will lead to suffering.
This mind cannot be stilled; the wise person should exhort themselves accordingly.
Therefore, when seeing an enemy, one should regard them as a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
By practicing such conduct, one shall attain happiness.
Thus all sentient beings, through their karma, lack self-mastery;
if mastery were achieved, who would willingly head toward suffering?
With a distracted mind focused on sensory objects, the heart is pierced by thorns without one’s awareness.
When food is cut off, anger increases; one turns even toward suffering with craving.
If one lacks meritorious conduct oneself, one instead craves the fetters of karma—like eating food mixed with poisonous medicine, one falls over the precipice of birth and death.
If one is oneself possessed of these afflictions, it is truly because one does not protect oneself;
wishing to liberate others, how can this possibly be achieved?
When the afflictions cause delusion and turbidity, they lead even to one's own destruction.
When poison is rampant and there is no compassion, how can one not guard against anger?
Since one's own nature is already deluded and confused, one causes disturbance to others;
there is no doubt that anger arises toward them, burning like fire.
When sentient beings are deluded in nature, the various faults they commit are such because of their ignorance and confusion,
like smoke熏 (xūn) [smoking] the void. If a person is angry and fails to guard themselves,
it is because of their ignorance, confusion, and lack of wisdom.
It is like one who, while wielding a staff to urge others on, only increases their anger and distress.
Because I, in past lives, caused suffering and distress to sentient beings,
I am now able to endure being subjected to suffering and distress in this present body.
My body is like iron, receiving the heating, hammering, and forging of others;
since this body is held like that iron, how could there be suffering?
Now I look upon this body as if it were a formless image.
Though afflicted by various sufferings, no anger should arise.
Fools and deluded ones give rise to the karma of craving; they do not know that suffering is their own root.
Since the conditions for suffering are one's own faults, why produce anger and affliction?

Just as one experiences the sufferings of hell, such as being among the flying birds in the Forest of Swords, one knows these arise from one's own karma; where, then, is there room for anger and vexation?
"I have acquired such karma"—knowing from where this fault originates, one should reflect thus.
Even if one enters hell, it is not due to the actions of others.
To exhaust my own karma, which is immeasurable and boundless—
since my karma is thus, I shall suffer in hell for a long time.
My faults are thus, yet he is truly my enemy;
how can one discern this and still, out of delusion, act with anger?
If a person guards themselves and remains patient without resentment when facing an enemy, [they will find peace].
When such mental qualities have arisen, how could one enter hell?
Even if I exhaust all my efforts, should I encounter such causes as those times,
if I cannot endure anger or protect myself, it will destroy my spiritual practice.
The mind is signless and formless; when distracted, it is immediately destroyed.
Because it is protected by the body, one should endure physical suffering.
Regarding the evil karma of speech, I shall not commit any of its many faults.
Since my body is not afflicted by manifold sufferings, why should the mind harbor anger?
Throughout this present life, I have practiced beneficial conduct with a pure heart;
since there is no longer any benefit [to be gained], what is the purpose of food and drink?
In all actions one undertakes, the essential point lies in benefiting others;
if there is no benefit or love therein, one will certainly incur sin without doubt.
It would be better to perish now than to possess a life of greedy and wicked existence.
Though one may live for a long time by wrong livelihood, at death one shall fall into the miserable realms.
It is like being in a dream where one enjoys happiness for a hundred years;
though it feels as if one has truly attained joy, upon waking, one knows it was but momentary and unreal.
It is like that time of impermanence; the lengthening or shortening of one’s lifespan—having realized these two matters, how could one find happiness?
Dwelling long in pleasure and amusement, one says to oneself, "I have gained much benefit."
Like a traveler who has been robbed, Naked and with empty hands;
as merit and benefit diminish with every transgression, The roots of sin arise once more.
Only when merit is exhausted will sin no longer arise, For one has thereby attained the benefit of non-anger.
What is the purpose of his livelihood, that he should perpetrate only unwholesome deeds?
Failing to reflect in this way, he destroys all that is good.
One should not praise anger, for it brings ruin to sentient beings.
When one’s mind is thus intent on benefiting others, there is no cause for anger to arise.
For those who cultivate their minds for the sake of others, if they cannot endure [offenses] and see afflictions arising in them, this is precisely what praises the merit of patience.
Regarding stupas, images, the sublime Dharma, and so forth— if they are reviled or destroyed—
the Buddhas and others feel no suffering or distress, nor do I harbor anger toward them.
Toward my teacher and his retinue, I shall not perform actions born of attachment.
Now, by reason of my past lives, I have seen this and exhort myself.
Observing sentient beings with an awakened mind, I see that they are constantly in the midst of manifold sufferings.
Having seen them thus, I am able to endure their suffering.
Hatred and delusion—these distinctions are equal to the fault itself;
regarding this poisonous transgression, how can one say there is no fault?
How could one, in the past, have committed the karma of harming others?
Such are the causes of these various karmas; why would one interrupt them?
Just as the merit of the Buddha is likewise, I now perform this with a single mind for the sake of all sentient beings, so that we may regard one another with hearts of loving-kindness.
It is like a fire burning its own house; when fire enters a house, if there is grass within it, that fire will naturally spread and creep along.
In this way, it is further illustrated by the mind: when it comes into contact with the fire of hatred, [it likewise spreads].
It burns away that merit and virtue, leaving nothing behind in an instant.
If one has a person in hand about to be killed, yet releases them—this is truly praiseworthy.
Since the sufferings of hell can thus be avoided, who would not praise such goodness?
If people in this world cannot endure even slight suffering,
how can they not sever their anger when facing the immeasurable sufferings of hell?
Because of such [anger], I have passed through hundreds of thousands of hells.
Each and every action is for the benefit of others, never performed for one's own sake.
I am free from such great sufferings and afflictions;
because I have transcended the world, I act in this way for the benefit of others.
Having abandoned suffering and attained happiness, they all praise his merit;
having received such praise as this, how could one not rejoice?
Since he has already obtained such unimpeded happiness, [how could one not rejoice]?
The practice of benefiting others is supreme; why does the wise person not strive for it?
If one does not cultivate such the most excellent conduct to attain happiness, and if this view is not abandoned, it will destroy right view.
If you desire to hold others dear, praise them for their virtues;
by praising the virtues of others, you truly hold them dear.
You should resolve to attain bodhicitta for the sake of all sentient beings.
Since they cause one to obtain all forms of happiness, why be angry with sentient beings?
The Buddha is the object of offerings for the three realms;
if you desire sentient beings to attain Buddhahood, yet worldly benefits are unattainable in reality, what use are those afflictions?
If one's own flesh and bones, as well as all one's kinsmen,
are as dear as one's own life, how can anger arise?
Just as one seeks awakening, one should employ the bodhicitta.
If one does not love sentient beings, why be angry when merit departs of its own accord?
If a person has something they seek and gives away great wealth in a vast act of generosity,
yet what was sought is not obtained, it would be better had the wealth remained in the house.
Regarding the merit and blessings of pure virtue, what obstacle prevents their attainment?
Having attained them, one does not enjoy them oneself, as if dwelling in anger while practicing.
Whether committing a transgression or performing a meritorious deed, one neither acts accordingly nor rejoices in them.
Furthermore, one does not rely on action; one should personally attain nothing at all.
If one loves an enemy and desires to seek their pleasure, or seeks their praise and acclaim, these things cannot be obtained through such means.
Though one desires to fulfill their benefit, it turns instead into suffering with no joy;
the Bodhicitta cannot endure this, for when benefit is not accomplished,
the evil hook of afflictions drags people away, depriving them of autonomy.
Just as the guardians of hell Cast people into boiling water and fire, I originally sought to benefit others; Why then do I crave empty praise?
Without merit, there is no long life; Without power, there is no peace or happiness.
If one's practice for self-benefit is not perfected, the wise should recognize this and proceed step by step toward its fulfillment; they should cherish and delight in its completion.
Such practice is worthy of praise, yet it is like taking up a blade to commit suicide.
Just as unreal things in the world Are neither beneficial nor bring joy,
So too, like a dilapidated house Where the sun shines through and is seen inside and out,
One must clearly understand That praise and blame are likewise unreal.
Reflect upon sound as being equal in its arising and ceasing;
with a mind such as this for the benefit of others, you should practice such conduct.
Whatever is received from others, act for their benefit.
Since they have already obtained happiness, my benefit is not in vain.
As each of them gains profit and joy, they praise me with all their might;
how could it be that I, in turn, lack distinct majesty and bliss?
When they praise me in this way, they gain [merit] through their own affection for me;
yet such a person lacks the necessary conditions, being like one who is foolish or deluded.
Although I receive this praise, I shall quickly break it apart and not become attached to it.
Those who hate right virtue act out of anger because of this;
they praise what constitutes an obstacle and prevent me from giving rise to it.
To protect them from falling into the evil realms, I practice non-self for their sake.
If one understands that all sentient beings are bound by gain, honor, and social status,
and seeks to bring those beings to liberation— how could such a person feel anger?
If someone desires to abandon suffering and enters the gateway to liberation, [how could one be angry with them?]
"This is the majestic power of the Buddha; why should I harbor anger toward him?
I shall not yield to this anger, for it is an obstacle to merit.
By practicing impartial patience, there is nothing that one cannot attain."
Through patience, one does not commit the various faults of oneself;
because faults are not committed, one attains merit.
Even if a person possesses no prior merit, if they give rise to patience within themselves, [merit will arise].
Always cause them to abide securely in patience; why then speak of obstacles?
Those who seek benefit in the world do not create obstacles to giving;
yet because they obstruct the going forth, one does not attain the going forth.
That which is difficult for the world to obtain, one who seeks it can give;
I speak only of this wholesome benefit, wherein no fault is found.
By means of that bodhisattva practice, one remains far removed from all enemies.
Just as one emerges from a treasury within a house, it is therefore said to be not difficult.
By repenting for karmic causes, with that initial act serving as the precursor,
one thus attains birth within the fruit of patience.
With a mind free from the notion of "mine," this mind abides in patience;
having accomplished the inconceivable, it makes offerings to the sublime Dharma.
This mind acts for the benefit of others, even at the cost of one's life.
Or perhaps because an enemy does not provide offerings, how can one speak of patience separately?
Toward each and every malicious mind, one should individually practice forbearance;
by attaining such patience, one thereby makes an offering to the sublime Dharma.
The Buddha-land and the realm of sentient beings—this is what the Great Muni has taught.
By performing many services toward them, one can bring about wealth and honor.
The Tathāgata and the Dharma are equal to all sentient beings.
Out of respect for the Buddha, one likewise respects sentient beings.
With such a resolve, one does nothing for oneself;
because of that great equality, one is equal toward all sentient beings.
With a mind of loving-kindness, one should make offerings to sentient beings;
the merit arising from such a resolve is equal to the merit of a Buddha, and through that merit, the state of a Buddha may be attained.
Therefore, the practice of the Buddha-dharma consists in regarding all sentient beings as equal to the Buddha.
The Buddha has no [concept of] equality; the ocean of his merit is boundless.
The Buddha’s merit is pure and refined; no merit can compare to it.
Though the three realms offer him worship, they cannot perceive it even upon seeing him.
The Teacher of the Buddha-dharma and the like is the supreme sentient being;
one should cultivate this mental orientation while making offerings to all sentient beings.
Toward one's own kinsmen, however, one is unable to initiate beneficial conduct.
In serving others, what fault could there be in doing so?
Even if it leads to the destruction of one’s body and entry into the Avīci Hell, if another has done such a thing, I shall do it as well;
with a vast mind for the sake of all beings, I shall thus constantly practice virtuous deeds.
Just as worldly people act as masters, yet their own affairs do not accord with their desires, how could I become their son? My nature is such that I am not their slave.
It is like a metaphor for the Buddha entering suffering yet remaining without suffering; as if having attained bliss, he is further filled with joy.
To bring such joy to all Buddhas, the Buddha’s own joy enables him to perform this deed for their sake.
Just as afflictions are universally present within my own body, may I fulfill all the needs of those who lack;
it is likewise with the suffering of sentient beings, yet I possess no skillful means and am left with nothing but empty compassion.
Therefore, I distance myself from this suffering; out of great compassion, I seek to rescue all beings from their pain.
Having previously provoked and vexed those who practice patience, I now repent of those transgressions.
I now serve the Tathāgata, just like any servant in the world;
though the feet of all people tread upon my head, I accept this with joy, being equal to the Buddha.
He performs all manner of lowly tasks in the world, yet out of compassion he encounters no hindrance;
seeing this peerless form of his, who would not revere such a Noble One?
Thus it is for the sake of honoring the Tathāgata; thus it is for the accomplishment of my own benefit;
thus it is for the removal of the world's suffering and affliction; thus do I now go forth into homelessness.
Just as a single king’s official is able to subdue a great multitude,
yet the multitude cannot subdue him alone because he is the king’s long-standing attendant;
that one is not solitary, for he possesses the power of the king.
Restraining oneself, one is neither timid nor inferior, and remains free from fault.
Abiding in patience with a heart of compassion, one possesses strength like that of a hell-warden;
yet one protects sentient beings as if serving a cruel king.
Hatred is not commanded by a king; like the suffering of those in hell, it is the afflictions that cause sentient beings to experience that suffering themselves.
Joy is not bestowed by a king; it is like attaining the state of a Buddha and the like.
A virtuous mind toward sentient beings—why do you not adopt this mind?
By protecting sentient beings, you shall later attain Buddhahood;
seeing that it inspires respect and praise, why do you not perceive this virtue?
Free from illness and endowed with beauty, Joyful and long-lived, wealthy and noble as a Wheel-Turning King— All these are attained through patience.
The wise practice forbearance; Enlightenment dwells in diligence.
Laziness distances one from merit, Just as the absence of wind prevents movement.
How can the power of diligence be understood?
That must be explained through analysis: Laziness and lack of diligence Should be viewed by oneself as poison.
Craving the taste of sleep, one deems it pleasure and freedom from affairs;
yet the suffering of saṃsāra is loathsome, for it arises from indolence.
This dwelling-place of afflictions is entered through the power of indolence.
Having already reached the gateway of impermanence, how is it that you do not know this now?
Exerting diligence for the sake of yourself and others—this practice you have not seen;
instead, you are indolent and fall asleep, like an ox in a butcher’s stall.
If one does not perceive this, all paths are severed;
since there is nothing to be attained, why do you delight in sleep?
Even if one attains a state of dignified deportment, impermanence will suddenly arrive.
Generosity is beyond reach; why dwell in indolence?
If one does not cultivate diligence, though remaining at ease as if diligent, one will suddenly encounter impermanence;
reflecting upon this, it is nothing but suffering.
Beholding that gate of Yama, filled with suffering and intense distress, tears fall in an instant;
though his kinsmen are present, they cannot save him.
Hearing the cries from the hells, he reflects upon the torment of his own karma.
Dwelling in this impure place, one’s terror is never-ending.
The sufferings of hell are most extreme; why then perform evil deeds again?
Like a fish still alive within a boiling cauldron, such is the fear they endure.
Having committed the karma for hell, one then undergoes the suffering of boiling water and fire;
with the body mangled and in agony, how can one attain purity?
The Mara King, who inflicts much suffering upon people, seizes them and delivers them to the Unconditioned (Death).
Impermanence is suffering and fearful; this is seen as the fruit of indolence.
The fool, deluded and attached to sleep, commits this fault which is no small matter:
he enters the great river of suffering and shall not again obtain a human body.
Setting aside the supreme Dharma, which is the seed of boundless bliss, you take pleasure in indolence and frivolity; why do you find joy in the causes of suffering?
Seeing that the power of anger is great, know that it is through one's own diligence that it is overcome.
The practices of self and others are equal for both self and other.
How could I attain bodhi? There is no action performed through discrimination;
by means of the Tathāgata’s reality, there is true liberation through truthful speech.
Even those mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, And insects such as shrimp and clams,
If they were to attain the power of diligence, They too would surely realize awakening.
How much more so for me, born as a human, Who am able to discern what is beneficial and what is not?
If one constantly understands all forms of diligence, how could one fail to attain Bodhi?
Whether it be the giving away of hands and feet, or the arising of fear therein—those who are deluded and ignorant violate the Teacher’s instructions; they do not understand this benefit for others.
Torn asunder, destroyed, and scorched— having been pulled out from all these boundless sufferings for countless koṭis of kalpas, yet he did not attain bodhi.
Having endured such immeasurable hardships for a long time, he finally realized bodhi.
It is like the pain caused by poison: when the poison is exhausted, the suffering departs entirely.
Acting as a physician for all, one heals the suffering of various ailments;
thus, suffering is eliminated, and all diseases are diminished.
Therefore, it is said that in providing medical treatment, sweet medicine does not benefit the illness;
the superior physician treats a great disease by never administering sweet medicine.
This is true from beginning to end, and it is practiced by all who possess wisdom.
Advancing progressively in practice, one gives away even one's own flesh.
When the wise contemplate this flesh of the body, they regard it as being like a vegetable that has grown;
once withered and discarded into the soil, such renunciation is not called difficult.
If suffering is produced by the body, the mind regards it as a vain occurrence;
when the wise person’s mind is not evil, they suffer no pain from evil karma.
Knowing the Dharma brings joy to the mind, and possessing merit brings joy to the body.
Without this, there is empty saṃsāra; how could one feel compassion for those who suffer?
To exhaust past sins and to deeply cultivate the ocean of merit for others—this power of bodhicitta is essential and urgent even for those of the two vehicles.
Thus, one who does not delight in such benefit—how could their practice lead to suffering?
The wise ride upon the palanquin of the bodhicitta and thereby attain happiness.
For the sake of accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings, they joyfully employ the power of skillful means.
Regarding the exertion of physical strength, suffering, and fear, one contemplates them only with praise.
By severing such conceptual discriminations, one increases diligence;
thus, my body is able to be relinquished, transcending the conventional means of the body.
I shall eliminate the countless faults of myself and others;
may each and every fault be exhausted without remainder, even as at the end of an eon.
When those faults are individually extinguished, may not even a hair’s breadth of them remain in me.
Having already been liberated from boundless suffering, how could my mind be diminished?
Seeking manifold merit for the benefit of both myself and others,
I shall study each and every virtue until the end of the eon, and my learning shall never cease.
Not even a hair’s breadth of merit have I ever performed in my life;
were I to be reborn, it would be in vain and devoid of substance.
I delight in making great offerings to worship the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Because of poverty one cannot act, and thus one's aspirations remain unfulfilled.
One does not bestow security upon those who fear, nor cultivate happiness for their mothers;
like entering a mother’s womb, the mother suffers only the pain of illness.
In the past I practiced the Dharma of renunciation, and now I have attained its fruit;
since my birth has been such as this, what further practice of the Dharma should I perform?
You are the root of all wholesome minds, the Muni of the world.
Those whose faculties never regress always obtain excellent karmic rewards.
Bound by the afflictions and suffering, they encounter various terrors;
through obstacles to their attachment to others, they commit transgressions that they themselves must experience.
If a person, in various places, is able to give rise to virtuous aspirations,
they will experience corresponding blessings and obtain the fruit of offerings.
If a person, in various places, commits transgressions while seeking pleasure, [they will receive the corresponding retribution].
Thus one experiences various retributions, And is beset by the afflictions of suffering.
The coolness within the Moon-Treasury, Its vast, wondrous fragrance and purity,
And the flavor of the Buddha’s voice, supreme— These cannot be obtained without cultivation.
Yet that son of the Sugata has attained understanding of the Sugata’s Dharma;
like a lotus emerging most excellently, he is also like the moon of the Benevolent Awakened One.
The executioners of Yama drag away the souls of the deceased, yet he remains unshaken.
Into fiery pits and molten bronze, they shall all enter to be burned and boiled;
amidst blazing flames and murderous weapons, their flesh shall be hacked by hundreds of thousands of catties;
falling upon the ground of glowing iron—all this results from many unwholesome deeds.
Therefore, cultivate goodness with the mind, And examine with extreme subtlety;
Relying upon that Vajra-banner, Train yourself and practice contemplation.
When first learning, contemplate their union; Do not fail to observe them as you train.
Yet you lack the name of the Supreme; you must turn your mind and act accordingly.
Whatever you do within this life only increases the suffering of sin;
if you do not cultivate the highest undertaking, you will seek nothing superior in your lower state.
One should know these three things: through the power of karma and afflictions, the causes of future evil are produced; how could one act in this way?
Worldly afflictions bind people, leaving them without freedom.
Just as a person is incapable [of acting], so too I have no agency.
Regarding the lower karma that is cultivated, how can one cause it to abide?
One should contemplate "I" and "non-self," yet this is what is performed by "mine."
A single drop of nectar, when consumed by a bird, transforms it into a Garuda;
yet in my mind, I consider this [merit] to be slight and inferior, for it can only liberate one from minor hardships.
Anger creates the hardship of being mindless, due to the fault of unwholesome karma.
The arising of the vision of non-mind is vast, supreme, and difficult to equal.
Therefore, with a pure mind, I compose these verses so that others may know:
"I am far removed from the conceptual proliferation of the three realms."
I have conquered all; no one can conquer me.
Now I know for myself that I am a son of the Buddha, a lion.
Sentient beings who are free from the notions of "self" and "person" attain the supreme state.
One does not conquer the enemy of indolence; rather, the enemy of indolence conquers oneself.
Drawn by the miserable realms, one’s bodily virtues are swiftly destroyed;
due to the folly and wickedness of one's attendants, one lives on handouts and suffers emaciation.
He accepts everything, yet dwells in the practice of pride;
though he has gained renown, how can such a base person be called noble?
If one is thus courageous, one will conquer those enemies within oneself.
One who practices this with such valor cannot be defeated by the enemy of pride.
If that prideful mind should arise, it is truly my own enemy;
though the supreme fruit desires to be born, that fruit will be entirely abandoned.
One who is like a lion of diligence, when seen among the beasts of affliction—
though there be thousands of millions of such beasts, they cannot prevail against him.
Though the world is filled with great suffering and distress, each person perceives it fully for themselves.
If the afflictions are not subdued, one shall undergo such suffering as this.
I would rather have my head fall off, and even have my heart and entrails torn out,
than fail to subdue all these enemies that are the afflictions.
By practicing this diligence, one exhausts those karmas of pride and attains a superior retribution,
experiencing the joy of spontaneous play for oneself. Yet,
though they cultivate the causes for happiness, they do not obtain it.
If one's practice is uncertain, one will likewise fail to attain excellence.
Craving for saṃsāra is never satisfied; it is like craving honey on the edge of a blade.
If one craves the nectar of merit, it becomes even more delicious as one consumes it.
Therefore, when karma is stilled, it brings forth wondrous fruits in accordance with one's conduct;
just as the sun is warm and the moon is cool, day and night follow one another.
The power of diligence is able to destroy indolence.
Having attained seclusion, one takes delight with a profound mind.
The staff of afflictions is firm and strong; one fights it with the sword of mindfulness and wisdom.
This is like the metaphor of a staff and a sword clashing, which is the same as the training of a woman.
The hand that grasps the sword lacks strength; losing it brings sudden terror.
To think of losing the sword is likewise so; hell dwells within the mind.
Those known in the world as virtuous persons would never willingly drink poisonous blood.
The transgressions of the mind are likewise thus; one should not commit mental transgressions.
With a mind of diligent effort in the homeless life, it is like holding a bowl of oil:
if the bowl were to fall, one would surely die; because of the risk of dropping it, there is great alarm and fear.
To be attached to sleep and indolence is like having a venomous snake in one's lap;
if it is not removed, one will surely be harmed, so its removal must be urgent.
Each of these profound faults requires that one turn the mind back toward contemplation.
This fault must not be tolerated; how could I commit it again?
With the sword of right mindfulness, I shall sever the causal karma of conditioned co-arising.
How is it that one attains this mindfulness known as the "state of self-mastery"?
When the mind of right mindfulness does not arise, even the slightest [affliction] cannot be extinguished;
as one's future karma follows from past deeds, all retributions are fully received.
It is like that tūla-cotton, which comes and goes with the wind.
So it is for the person of diligence; Thus they attain the supreme [state].

Compiled in verse by the Holy Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna;
translated at the monastery of Buddhaprītivīryavardhana in Jālandhara, Central India.
Abiding in the state of meditative concentration, the mind is settled.
Compassionate toward those whose minds are distracted, dwelling amidst the sprouts of affliction;
I now know my own body and mind, and thus no distraction arises.
For this reason, I remain far removed from the world and likewise free from doubt.
Beneficial conduct is dear, yet craving does not leave the world;
therefore, the wise reflect upon this and relinquish it all.
Relying upon śamatha, vipaśyanā, and so forth...
Arising and practicing in this way, one destroys the afflictions.
First seek śamatha; do not rely on worldly practices.
Since impermanence is ever-present, what need is there for craving?
If one sees through a thousand lifetimes, one no longer gives rise to craving or attachment;
one does not delight in *vaibhāṣya*, nor does one dwell in meditative equipoise (*samādhi*).
Having seen this, one is not yet satisfied, for this is the affliction of past thirst.
If one does not see things as they truly are, how can one exhaust the afflictions?
When the mind conditions the accumulation of craving, it is scorched by the afflictions;
contemplating such a state leads to downfall, for life is short and lasts but a moment.
Virtuous friends do not remain for long; if one does not achieve the steadfast Dharma, their conduct will be the same as that of the deluded, and they will certainly fall into the evil realms.
How could one associate with the deluded? For they are drawn away by portions of poison.
Yet toward one's own kin, one may in an instant incur resentment.
Ordinary beings are of a different nature; their joy and anger are unstable.
They are difficult to serve due to their frequent anger, and they distance themselves from wholesome benefits.
With an inferior mind, one praises oneself; bound by attachment and the sin of hatred, one does not abandon anger and shall fall into the evil realms.
Deluded and failing to restrain the mind, for this reason one possesses no merit.
Praising oneself and disparaging others, one finds pleasure within saṃsāra.
This is the way of the deluded; by abiding in such unwholesome states, one attains all manner of discordant and unvirtuous results.
Delighting in my own person, yet with no craving in my mind,
and remaining far removed from delusion, I shall receive loving service.
Not for the sake of praise, but abiding in whatever wholesome deeds there may be.
Briefly, like a bee producing honey, I achieve accomplishment through tranquility.
In all my movements, as if I were someone never seen before,
I am constantly praised and loved by many people.
If one is deluded in every situation, yet finds pleasure and happiness therein,
one will thereby incur the fear of birth and death within this world.
Therefore, that wise person fears birth and death.
Knowing the thousandfold kinds of suffering, one dwells [in them] and must certainly undergo them.
Yet, if for even a single moment one cultivates diligence for oneself,
one will obtain a good reputation as well as abundant offerings.
When those who share my purpose disparage me for lacking merit, if they thus heap such insults upon me, I consider it praise and rejoice.
Though disparaged, I do not feel anger; though praised, I do not feel delight.
Whether it be the Buddha or sentient beings, all things are thus in their various forms.
Praising them brings merit, while slandering them invites bitter retribution;
that the world does not contemplate this is due to its ignorance.
Inherently suffering and dwelling together, what joy can there be in such birth?
That the deluded are not friends—this is what the Tathāgata has taught.
If one dwells among the deluded, there is nothing that does not bring self-interest.
If one enters the gateway of benefiting others, this is what constitutes self-love.
